parole.significato: Marks singular nouns, with a foundation in Greek or Latin, often implying femininity, especially when contrasted with w…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin -a (nominative first declension neuter singular suffix)

parole.significato: toward
parole.testo: Derived from Latin ad (“at”), from Proto-Italic *ad, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd. Coined by British anatomist John Barclay.

parole.significato: Of, near, or pertaining to; adjective suffix appended to various words, often nouns, to make an adjective form. Often a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -āris (“of, pertaining to”). Distant doublet of -al.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to. Adjectival suffix appended to various words, often nouns, to produce an adjective form. Often adde…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English -arie, a back-formation from Latin and French-borrowed adjectives ending respectively in -ārius and -aire (more rarely from Latin adjectives in -āris: see exemplary and lapidary). Doublet of -ar, -eer, -ier, and -yer; see also the related -arian.

parole.significato: forms adjectives with meaning "having the specified thing"
parole.testo: First attested in the 15th century; borrowed from Latin -ātus, the perfect passive participle ending of first conjugation verbs, also used to form participial adjectives from nouns. Before -ate was introduced as a suffix in Middle English, Latin-borrowed participial adjectives were written with fina

parole.significato: derives or adapts verbs (mostly) from Latin stems
parole.testo: See Etymology 1. In Middle English, verbs were derived from Latin-borrowed participial adjectives (also used as their past participles) and formed their infinitives in -aten (see -en; Middle English desolaten for modern desolate). In the 15th century, the loss of most verbal morphology made verbs fo

parole.significato: forms nouns denoting a rank or office
parole.testo: From the Latin abstract-noun-forming suffix -ātus, -ātūs.

parole.significato: A process of becoming (growing or increasing in the trait specified by the prefixed stem).
parole.testo: From Latin -escens, form of -ēscō (“I become”). By surface analysis, -esce + -ence.

parole.significato: Holder or bearer of something.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin -fer (“bearer”).

parole.significato: Used in forming placenames, especially of countries.
parole.testo: From Latin -ia and Ancient Greek -ία (-ía), -εια (-eia), which form abstract nouns of feminine gender.

parole.significato: Any of a group of related compounds - azide, polysaccharide, glycoside.
parole.testo: Generalized in the early 19th c. from oxide (which has its ending from French acide, itself from Latin -idus in acidus), and gradually displaced earlier -uret, both introduced in the English translation of de Morveau, Lavoisier et al.'s 1787 book Méthode de nomenclature chimique.

parole.significato: Creating or causing something.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin -(i)ficus. By surface analysis, -ify + -ic.

parole.significato: Tending to, or capable of.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin -ilis.

parole.significato: Used to form the names of metal elements, after the style of early-named elements, as well as the isotopes of hydrogen.
parole.testo: From Latin -um (neuter singular morphological suffix), based on Latin terms for metals such as ferrum (“iron”).

parole.significato: Used to form nouns of quality, state, or condition.
parole.testo: From Latin -or.

parole.significato: Forming diminutive nouns.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -ula. Doublet of -ule.

parole.significato: Tasting sour or bitter.
parole.testo: Attested since the 17th century, from Latin acerbus (“sour, bitter”).

parole.significato: Doing, enacting, forming a verb.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ad-. Doublet of at-.

parole.significato: The evolution of a mimic to resemble its model more closely.
parole.testo: Coined by evolutionary biologists L. P. Brower and J. van Z. Brower in 1972 for the paper "Parallelism, convergence, divergence, and the new concept of advergence in the evolution of mimicry" on the pattern of convergence, substituting ad- for con- to emphasize the one-sidedness of the approach. Bor

parole.significato: The pouring of liquid, especially as a hydrotherapy.
parole.testo: From Latin affusio, from Latin affundō (“to pour or sprinkle onto”), from Latin fundō (“to pour”), from Proto-Italic *hundō (“to pour out”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰewd- (“to pour”).

parole.significato: A temporally organized plan for matters to be attended to.
parole.testo: From Latin agenda (“things that ought to be done”), future passive participle (gerundive) of agō (“to do, act, make”).

parole.significato: One who exerts power, or has the power to act.
parole.testo: From Latin agēns, present active participle of agere (“to drive, lead, conduct, manage, perform, do”).

parole.significato: Agriculture.
parole.testo: Originally from Latin ager, agrī (“field”), reinforced by English agriculture, of the same etymology. Doublet of acre.

parole.significato: agriculture
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin ager.

parole.significato: In Ancient Rome, a white tablet or register on which the praetor's edicts and other public notices were recorded.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin album (“blank white writing tablet”), from albus (“white”).

parole.significato: Of a voice or instrument, high pitch; especially, the octave above the top line of the treble stave.
parole.testo: From Latin altus (“high”). Doublet of old and alto.

parole.significato: The basic impulses and instincts which govern one's actions.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin animus (“the mind, in a great variety of meanings: the rational soul in man, intellect, consciousness, will, intention, courage, spirit, sensibility, feeling, passion, pride, vehemence, wrath, etc., the breath, life, soul”), from Proto-Italic *anamos, from Proto-Indo-Eur

parole.significato: anus
parole.testo: Derived from Latin ānus.

parole.significato: Nervous and worried.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin anxius, from angō (“to cause pain, choke”); akin to Ancient Greek ἄγχω (ánkhō, “to choke”). See anger; angst.

parole.significato: The highest or the greatest part of something, especially forming a point.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin apex (“point, tip, summit”).

parole.significato: water
parole.testo: From Middle English aqua (“water”), borrowed from Latin aqua

parole.significato: Sharp; perceptive; shrewd.
parole.testo: From Latin argūtus, perfect passive participle of arguō (“to clarify”).

parole.significato: touching; adjacent
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin attingēns (“touching”, passive participle), from Latin attingō (“to touch; to come into contact with”, verb). Further from Latin tangō (“to touch, to grasp”, verb), from Proto-Italic *tangō and Proto-Indo-European *teh₂g-, both verbs of the same meaning.

parole.significato: bird
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin avis (“bird”).

parole.significato: An imaginary line around which an object spins (an axis of rotation) or is symmetrically arranged (an axis of symmetry).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin axis (“axle, axis”) in the 16th century. Via Latin cognate with ala, aisle, atelier. Via Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱs- cognate with inherited English axle and borrowed axo-, axon.

parole.significato: Two in number.
parole.testo: PIE word  *dwóh₁ Borrowed from Latin bi-, from Proto-Italic *dwi-, from Proto-Indo-European *dwi-. Doublet of twi- and di-.

parole.significato: Very absorbent.
parole.testo: From Latin bibulus from bibō (“drink”) + -ulus from Proto-Italic *pibō, from Proto-Indo-European *píph₃eti, from root *peh₃- (“drink”); whence also imbibe and beverage via Old French beivre.

parole.significato: Something extra that is good; an added benefit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bonus (“good”). Doublet of bona.

parole.significato: Any of several, often thorny shrubs or small trees, especially
parole.testo: Calque of Latin cervī spīna (“deer's thorny shrub”), cervi (“deer's”) being the genitive singular of cervus (“deer”), from Proto-Italic *kerwos, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥h₂wós, from *ḱerh₂- (“horn”) + *-wós, spīna (“thorny shrub”) from Proto-Italic *speinā, from Proto-Indo-European *spey- (“shar

parole.significato: Warm, hot.
parole.testo: From Latin calidus (“hot”), from caleō (“to be warm or hot; glow”) + -idus, from Proto-Italic *kalēō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelh₁-. Cognate with Italian calido (“hot”), French chaud (“warm, hot”), Portuguese cálido (“warm”), and Spanish cálido (“warm”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Caprinae (goats, sheep, and certain wild relatives).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caprīnus. The taxonomic sense is a semantic loan from translingual Caprinae.

parole.significato: look out!; beware!
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cavē, second-person singular present active imperative of caveō (“to beware”). Used at Eton College, Berkshire.

parole.significato: Referring to an Indo-European language that did not produce sibilants from a series of Proto-Indo-European palatovelar…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin centum (“hundred”), attested at least since 1890s. Its use in linguistics is due to it being a canonical example of a word retaining an original velar stop, as opposed to Avestan 𐬯𐬀𐬙𐬆𐬨 (satəm). Doublet of hundred and satem.

parole.significato: A short microscopic hairlike organelle projecting from a eukaryotic cell (such as a unicellular organism or one cell of…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cilium (“eyelid”).

parole.significato: Together: the root word is done co-incidently.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin co-, from con-, from Proto-Italic *kom-, from *kom, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm, possibly from *ḱe.

parole.significato: A sharecropping tenant farmer of the late Roman Empire and Early Middle Ages.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin colōnus.

parole.significato: Against; in opposition to.
parole.testo: From Latin contrā (“against”). Doublet of counter-.

parole.significato: To give something that is or becomes part of a larger whole.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes From Latin contribūtus, perfect passive participle of contribuō (“to bring together; to unite”), from con- (“together”) + tribuō (“to bestow”), from tribus (“tribe”), derived from trēs (“three”), from Proto-Italic *trēs, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes.

parole.significato: The basal segment of a limb of various arthropods (insects and spiders, for example).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin coxa, from Proto-Italic *koksā, from Proto-Indo-European *kóḱseh₂, from *koḱs- (“joint, limb”) + *-eh₂. Doublet of cuisse.

parole.significato: That which is believed; accepted doctrine, especially religious doctrine; a particular set of beliefs; any summary of p…
parole.testo: From Middle English crede, from Old English crēda, crēdo, from Latin crēdō (“to believe”), from Proto-Italic *krezdō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱréd-dʰeh₁-ti (“to trust, believe”, literally “to place one's heart”), a compound phrase of the oblique case form of *ḱḗr (“heart”). Creed is cognate with O

parole.significato: In a natural, untreated state.
parole.testo: Doublet of crudo, which was borrowed from Italian, and (more distantly) raw through Proto-Indo-European.

parole.significato: Used in indicating a thing or person which has two or more roles, functions, or natures, or which has changed from one…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cum.

parole.significato: Any of the subdivisions of a tribe in ancient Rome
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin curia.

parole.significato: Bent without angles; crooked; curved.
parole.testo: Attested since the 1690s, from Latin curvus (“bent, curved”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to bend, curve, turn”) + *-wós. Doublet of curb, shrink, carcer, and cancer.

parole.significato: harm; detriment
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin damnum.

parole.significato: reversal, undoing
parole.testo: From Latin dē-, from the preposition dē (“of”, “from”). For sense development, compare Old English æf-, which was a similar prefix.

parole.significato: Easily damaged or requiring careful handling.
parole.testo: From Middle English delicat, from Latin dēlicātus (“giving pleasure, delightful, soft, luxurious, delicate, (in Medieval Latin also) fine, slender”), from dēlicia + -ātus (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), usually in plural dēliciae (“pleasure, delight, luxury”), from dēliciō (“to allure, entice

parole.significato: Right; on the right; toward the right.
parole.testo: From Latin dexter (“right”).

parole.significato: A university professor, particularly one at Oxford or Cambridge.
parole.testo: From Latin dominus (“lord, head of household”), akin to Italian don, Sicilian don, Spanish don; from domus (“house”). Doublet of dom, domine, dominie, and dominus.

parole.significato: To endow.
parole.testo: First attested in c. 1540; borrowed from Latin dōtātus, perfect passive participle of Latin dōtō (“to endow, apportion”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dōs (“dowry, gift”, oblique stem in dōt-) + -ō, from Proto-Italic *dōtis, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₃tis, from Proto-Indo-European *deh₃-

parole.significato: two
parole.testo: PIE word  *dwóh₁ Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Italic *duō Latin duo English duo- From Latin duo (“two”).

parole.significato: Used to form terms with the sense of something being absent, being removed, or moving outward.
parole.testo: From Latin ē-.

parole.significato: The self, especially with a sense of self-importance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ego (“I”). Chosen by Freud’s translator as a translation of his use of German Ich as a noun for this concept from the pronoun ich (“I”). Doublet of I and Ich.

parole.significato: Equal, equally.
parole.testo: From Latin aequi-, from aequus. See also equ-.

parole.significato: the place the train originated from or called at prior to the present location.
parole.testo: From Latin ex (“out of, from”); originated as a telegraphic abbreviation.

parole.significato: Outside of, beyond.
parole.testo: From Latin extra (“outside, except, beyond”, adverb and preposition), from exter (“being on the outside”).

parole.significato: The time, or the condition, of budding or flowering.
parole.testo: From Latin florēscō, from flōreō (“to bloom, flower”) + -ēscō, from flōs (“flower”), from Proto-Italic *flōs, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃- (“flower, blossom”), from *bʰel- (“to bloom”), as if through the form flōrēscentia.

parole.significato: An instrument used in surgery or medical procedures for grasping and holding objects, similar to tongs or pincers.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin forceps.

parole.significato: Synonym of frenulum.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin frēnum (“bridle, curb, bit”).

parole.significato: A cone or pyramid whose tip has been truncated by a plane parallel to its base.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin frustum (“morsel”).

parole.significato: Of or related to lightning, particularly (historical) in reference to its use in divination.
parole.testo: From Latin fulguralis, from fulgur (“lightning”) + -ālis (“-al: forming adjectives”), from Proto-Italic reconstructed as *folgos and related to the idea of flashing or lightening.

parole.significato: A thief.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fur (“thief”).

parole.significato: A legally defined unit of Roman society, being a collection of people related through a common ancestor by birth, marri…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gēns (“gens; people, tribe”), from Proto-Italic *gentis, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénh₁tis (“birth; production”), from *ǵenh₁- (“to beget; to give birth; to produce”) + *-tis (suffix forming abstract or action nouns from verb roots). Doublet of kind, genesis, and jati. See also

parole.significato: A category in the classification of organisms, ranking below family (Lat. familia) and above species.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin genus (“birth, origin, a race, sort, kind”) from the root gen- in Latin gignō (“to beget, produce”). Doublet of gender and genre, further related to kin.

parole.significato: To gape; to cause a hiatus.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin hiō, hiāre, hiāvī, hiātum.

parole.significato: A human.
parole.testo: From Latin homō̆ (“a human being, man, person”), sometimes as a shortening of Homo sapiens. Doublet of gome, hombre, ombre, and omi.

parole.significato: not; a form of the prefix in-, used before l
parole.testo: From Latin il-, assimilated form of in- before l-.

parole.significato: Expressing negation; not.
parole.testo: From Latin im-, assimilated form of in- used before b-/p-/m-.

parole.significato: To drink (used frequently of alcoholic beverages).
parole.testo: From Middle English imbiben, from Latin imbibō, from im- + bibō (“to drink”) (whence also beverage), from Proto-Italic *pibō, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₃-, whence also potable, potion.

parole.significato: Used with certain words to reverse their meaning.
parole.testo: PIE word  *né From Middle English in-, borrowed (in words of latinate origin) from Latin in- (“not”). Sometimes the Latin word has passed through French before reaching English (e.g. incapable, incertainty, inclement, incompatible). Doublet of un-.

parole.significato: Behaving as though affected by alcohol including exhilaration, and a dumbed or stupefied manner.
parole.testo: From Latin inēbriātus, past participle of inēbriō (“intoxicate”) from in- + ēbrius (“drunk, intoxicated”) from Proto-Italic *ēɣʷrios, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ēgʷʰ-ryo-s from root *h₁egʷʰ- (“drink”); whence also ebrious and inebriate.

parole.significato: To introduce (something) as a reasoned conclusion; to conclude by reasoning or deduction, as from premises or evidence.
parole.testo: From Latin inferō, from Latin in- (“in, at, on; into”) + Latin ferō (“bear, carry; suffer”) (cognate to Old English beran, whence English bear), from Proto-Italic *ferō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰéreti (“to bear, carry”), from the root *bʰer-. Literally “carry forward”, equivalent to “bear in”, as

parole.significato: To ask (about something).
parole.testo: From Latin inquīrō (“to seek for”), composed of in- (“in, at, on; into”) + quaerō (“to seek, look for”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Italic *kʷaizeō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂- (“to acquire”). Displaced Middle English enqueren (from Old French enquerre, of the same source) and

parole.significato: A number that is not a fraction; an element of the infinite and numerable set {..., -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ...}.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin integer (“whole”), from Proto-Italic *n̥tagros (“untouched”). Doublet of entier and entire. Related to English tact, thack, and thwack.

parole.significato: A position which is in between two (or more) of the kind indicated by the root.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin inter- (“between, amid”), a form of prepositional inter (“between”).

parole.significato: Used for expressing negation; not
parole.testo: From Latin ir-, assimilated form of in- used before r-.

parole.significato: An amusing story.
parole.testo: From Latin iocus (“joke, jest, pastime”), from Proto-Italic *jokos (“word, (playful?) saying”), from Proto-Indo-European *yokos (“word, utterance”), from ultimate root Proto-Indo-European *yek- (“to speak, utter”) (of which distant cognates include Proto-Celtic *yextis (“language”) (Breton yezh (“la

parole.significato: Synonym of by Jupiter.
parole.testo: From Latin Iūpiter (“father Jove”), from Proto-Italic *djous patēr (literally “sky father”) (cognate with Ancient Greek Ζεῦ πάτερ (Zeû páter, “father Zeus”)), from *djous (“day, sky”) + *patēr (“father”), from Proto-Indo-European *dyḗws (literally “the bright one”), from *dyew- (“to be bright, day s

parole.significato: A Roman or Latin law (particularly in ancient Rome or in medieval Europe).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin lēx, lēges (“law(s)”).

parole.significato: Synonym of tongue.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin lingua (“the tongue”). Doublet of langue and tongue.

parole.significato: A place or locality, especially a centre of activity or the scene of a crime.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin locus. Doublet of lieu.

parole.significato: Pruriently detailed and sensationalistic about something shocking or horrifying, especially with regard to violence or…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lūridus (“pale yellow, wan”).

parole.significato: Greater in dignity, rank, importance, significance, or interest.
parole.testo: From Middle English major, from Latin maior, comparative of magnus (“great, large; noble, important”), from Proto-Indo-European *méǵh₂yōs (“greater”), comparative of *meǵh₂- (“great”). Compare West Frisian majoar (“major”), Dutch majoor (“major”), French majeur. Doublet of mayor. Noun sense 1 is a s

parole.significato: mother
parole.testo: From Latin māter.

parole.significato: The middle layer of the wall of a blood vessel or lymph vessel which is composed of connective and muscular tissue.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin media, the feminine nominative of medius (“middle”, adjective), from Proto-Italic *meðjos, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“between”). In the sense of a unit of dry measure, via Spanish media. Doublet of medium, medio, and mediate.

parole.significato: The means and institutions for publishing and broadcasting information.
parole.testo: Latinate plural of medium, particularly as a clipping of communications media and often reinterpreted as singular or mass noun, from Latin media, neuter plural form of medius (“middle”, adjective), from Proto-Italic *meðjos, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“between”).

parole.significato: The material of the surrounding environment, e.g. solid, liquid, gas, vacuum, or a specific substance such as a solvent.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin medium, neuter of medius (“middle”), from Proto-Italic *meðjos, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“between”). Compare middle. Doublet of mid, medio, media, and meson.

parole.significato: A keratin-filled cyst that can appear just under the epidermis or on the roof of the mouth.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin milium. Compare Middle English mile.

parole.significato: Of a body in motion: the tendency of a body to maintain its inertial motion; the product of its mass and velocity, or t…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mōmentum. Doublet of moment and movement.

parole.significato: A delay in bringing a claim.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin mora (“duration of time, delay”).

parole.significato: More than one; pertaining to more than one thing.
parole.testo: From late Middle English multi-, from Latin multī, from multus.

parole.significato: A wall, in the context of Ancient Rome. "Ubi vero moveri et adpropinquare muris viderunt, nova atque inusitata specie c…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mūrus (“wall”).

parole.significato: A cloud in outer space consisting of gas or dust (e.g. a cloud formed after a star explodes).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin nebula (“little cloud, mist”). First attested in 1655. Akin to Ancient Greek νεφέλη (nephélē, “cloud”), German Nebel (“mist, nebula”), Old Norse nifl, Polish niebo (“sky, heaven”), Russian не́бо (nébo, “sky”).

parole.significato: An aggregate of neurons.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nīdus (“nest”). Doublet of nye and nest.

parole.significato: Relating to pain and its perception.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin noceō (“hurt”). First used in nociception.

parole.significato: prevocalic form of nona-
parole.testo: From Latin nōnus (“ninth”).

parole.significato: The period of darkness in each twenty-four hours; a night.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin nox, from Proto-Italic *nok⁽ʷ⁾ts, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.

parole.significato: The core, central part of something, around which other elements are assembled.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin nucleus (“kernel, core”). The earliest uses refer to the head of a comet and the kernel of a seed, both recorded in Lexicon Technicum in 1704. The sense in atomic physics was coined by British scientist Michael Faraday in 1844 in a theoretical meaning.

parole.significato: Hatred; dislike.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin odium, from Proto-Italic *odjom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ed-.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a kitchen garden; used for culinary purposes.
parole.testo: From Latin olitōrius (“of or related to gardeners, produce, or vegetables”), from olitor (“gardener, seller of vegetables or herbs”), from olus + -itō (“forming frequentative verbs”) + -or (“-er: forming agent nouns”), variant of holus (“vegetable”), from Old Latin helus, believed to come from unatt

parole.significato: all
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin omnis (“all”).

parole.significato: A legal obligation.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin onus (literally “burden”).

parole.significato: A large, defended Iron Age settlement associated with the Celtic La Tène culture.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin oppidum (“(chiefly walled or fortified) town”).

parole.significato: A work of music or set of works with a specified rank in an ordering of a composer's complete published works.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin opus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the mouth.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin ōs (“the mouth”).

parole.significato: An opening or entrance to a passage, particularly one at either end of the cervix, internal (to the uterus) or external…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin ōs (“mouth”).

parole.significato: The female gamete in animals; the egg cell.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ōvum (“egg”). Doublet of egg, ey, huevo, and oeuf.

parole.significato: Eggcorn of onus; the condition of being obligated or responsible for something.
parole.testo: An eggcorn of onus, as owe (“to be under obligation”, verb) + -ness (abstract-noun suffix), interpretable as "the state of being under obligation." parole.significato: A country district with scattered hamlets.
